newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Ethiopia farm production not affected by drought.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopia farm production not affected by drought.

text.p: Drought that devastated most of East Africa from December to March will not affect Ethiopia's agricultural production, farm officials said on Thursday.
They told Reuters key growing areas for coffee, the Horn of African country's main commodity export, had "enjoyed perennial rains". Coffee is grown in western Ethiopia.
"The drought sweeping much of East Africa therefore has not touched Ethiopia's coffee growing areas and the country's main crop belts," a senior government official said.

With annual production of 200,000 to 250,000 tonnes, Ethiopia is Africa's third largest producer of coffee behind Uganda and Ivory Coast. Coffee officials say production is set to rise in 1996/97 and 1997/98 (July/June).
Government officials said nomads and pastoralists in the eastern and southern regions were the main victims of drought.

Ethiopian Metrological Office official Zwedu Tesema said drought-affected Ethiopian regions were the Somali-inhabited eastern region, south and north Omo, and Borena which are in the same weather belt as northern Kenya and northeastern Uganda.
Some 600,000 people in Ethiopia's Somali Region have been seriously affected by drought and require assistance. Emergency relief has been flowing there since March.
"Southern and northern Omo, Borena and the lowland of Somali region which encountered prolonged dryness have started to get rains since March," Zwedu told Reuters.
Zwedu said weather conditions in Ethiopia during the 1997/98 period were expected to help agriculture.

"Better and near normal rainfall distribution is expected over Ethiopia during the next crop year. However some pocket areas in the central, eastern and northern parts are expected to encounter deficiency," Zwedu added.

Ethiopia enjoyed good rains in 1996/97 and recorded a bumper harvest of 11.7 million tonnes of grains, which far exceeded the estimated 8.7 million tonnes of grains required to feed its 55 million people.
Ethiopian coffee officials have also forecast a bumper crop in 1996/97 and see exports reaching a record 108,000 tonnes.
Ethiopia exported 102,000 tonnes of coffee in 1995/96 and earned $279.5 million -- lower than the $300.9 million received for exporting 78,420 tonnes of coffee in 1994/95.
Ethiopia's irrigated sugar cane plantations, supplying the country's four sugar mills, receive water from the vast reserves of the Koka and Finchaa dams.

Ethiopia, with a total annual sugar production of nearly 400,000 tonnes, is expected to be a sugar exporting nation this year when its fourth and biggest sugar factory at Finchaa starts production in July, according to sugar officials.
Ethiopia has forecast gross domestic product growth of 8.0 percent in 1996/97 from 7.6 percent recorded in 1995/96.
The drought led to a downwards adjustment in forecasts for coffee and tea production in Kenya and Tanzania.
